title: Where the Locals Live: The Stack, Its Size, and the Recursion That Ends the Program

questions.question: A recursive function died with the shell reporting status 139. What is that number?
options: An exit code the program returned to mean out of memory
A CMake error code for a crashed test
128 plus signal 11, SIGSEGV, so the program did not choose to stop
The number of frames it managed before failing
questions.explanation: Lesson 00-09 has the arithmetic. A status above 128 almost always means a signal, which is why that range is not yours to use: a tool returning 139 on purpose cannot be told from one that crashed.

questions.question: A local one call deeper was at a lower address than its caller's, by 48 bytes. What does that tell you?
options: The second local was on the heap
48 bytes is the size of the local, not the frame
The stack grows downwards, so deeper means numerically smaller
The compiler reordered the locals, so addresses say nothing
questions.explanation: Which is the opposite of what the word deeper suggests. It is a property of the processor and holds on every toolchain this curriculum claims.

questions.question: A recursion with 64 byte frames reached depth 130860 on an 8 MiB stack. What should you conclude about the same code on Windows?
options: It has about an eighth of the room, since the Windows default stack is 1 MiB, so roughly 10900 safe levels instead of 87000
Nothing; the stack limit is a property of C++ and is the same everywhere
It is unaffected, because Windows grows the stack on demand without limit
It will be faster, since Windows frames are smaller
questions.explanation: The limit is a setting, not a property of the language: ulimit -s on Linux, fixed at link time on Windows. A recursion comfortable on one can end the program on the other.

questions.question: A 15625 KiB array was declared in main beside a branch that only used a std::vector. That branch crashed. Why?
options: The frame is allocated when the function is entered, not when the declaration is reached, so an unused local costs its full space
The compiler initialised the array before choosing the branch
The vector allocated on the stack because the array was nearby
It was a compiler bug; moving the array should change nothing
questions.explanation: Measured: moving the array into its own function made the vector branch survive with status 0. So several large locals in mutually exclusive branches can fail when no single branch would.

questions.question: double samples[n]; with n a runtime value. What do gcc and clang do under -Wall -Wextra?
options: Both warn about it, which -Werror would turn into an error
Both accept it silently, as a C99 extension; -Wvla or -pedantic-errors rejects it on both
Both reject it, since C++ has no variable length arrays
gcc rejects it and clang accepts it
questions.explanation: C++ has no VLAs; both compilers offer the C99 feature as an extension. The danger is not portability, it is that the size comes from the input, so the function is one input away from a stack overflow.

questions.question: Why does DepthGuard decrement in its destructor rather than at the end of the recursive function?
options: So the guard can be copied safely between calls
Destructors run faster than an explicit decrement
Because the counter must be decremented before the recursive call returns
An early return, a break or a throw all skip a line at the bottom and none of them skips a destructor; a counter that leaks reports a limit never reached
questions.explanation: This is lesson 02-03's point applied to recursion. The guard also deletes its copy operations, and checks/ proves it: copying one would count a level once and give it back twice.
